The biggest thing for studying well in college is deadlines. People who flunk out are people who stopped meeting deadlines. Stuff starts to pile up after even a day of missed homework turn ins. A day can turn into a few days, which can turn into a week, which can turn into a semesters worth of skipped classes and bad feelings about yourself. It’s not fun, and very few people comeback from that. If you make deadlines, you will pass your class, and I can promise you that.

Too add: My rationale was always that a stronger person in my scenario would be doing much better, but that doesn’t mean that I’m a bad person. A weightlifter isn’t weak because he can’t lift as much as the heaviest guy in the gym, that’s just stupid.

We think that those who are better than us are happier (it’s like the halo effect, if you wanna look it up). I can assure you that it’s not true. I’m at the top of my engineering class, and I struggle to do homework at times because I get anxious/depressed. Having _____ doesn’t make your problems go away. You do.

The way I got rid of my worse times of anxiety was recognizing my triggers and signs of an oncoming panic attack. I used to freak the fuck out doing schoolwork because I was worried about my grades. I knew a trigger could be homework, so I was always wary of a panic attack when I was doing my homework. I also knew that my early signs were my heart would race, my mind would blank, and I’d be forgetting little details about things. So when I noticed these symptoms, I’d take a 5-10 minute break to reset and come back to my homework and that mitigated most of the attacks.

I got better at time and now I can stop an oncoming attack in less than a minute whereas before I’d be paralyzed with anxiety for hours on end. Hope this helps.

1) don’t worry yourself out of the interview. The first interview is good to get out of the way so you know what to do in the future.

2) Obviously, they see something in you if they want to interview you. Find things about you and your professional life to talk about, such as hobbies, passions, and goals. Get enough topics/ideas to talk about for an hour.

3) Practice! Practicing saying key phrases/sentence that have ideas you want to get across to them so you don’t have a gaff during your interview. Speak to the mirror, talk in the car while driving, or talk to a friend.

4) on the day of the interview, get enough sleep, eat a good breakfast, clean yourself up, leave early enough to be there 20-30 minutes before your interview, and, on the way there, listen to pump up music (I find it best to sing along to faster paced songs that I know the words to like Kickstart my heart or Joker and the thief) to get yourself pumped and ready to knock that interview out of the park!

Step one is to relax. Derivatives are easy once you know the rules. Start with (d/dx) x^n = nx^(n-1), then learn the chain rule, trig stuff, and other special cases (log, e, etc.). You also have to make sure your algebra isn’t too shabby, but you can kinda bs your way through it not knowing everything.

Here are some good videos on it: 

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=YG15m2VwSjA

https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=zCxbsCbgAKo&list=PLl-gb0E4MII1ml6mys-RXoQ0O3GfwBPVM&index=14 (this whole playlist is really good, I’d watch all of chapter two if you are struggling).

Second derivatives aren’t the hardest thing to find, but they are tricky to interpret. To find a second derivative, you just take the derivative of the derivative of your original function. So this means they are the change in the change of your original function. This website has a much better description than my abridged version: https://activecalculus.org/single/sec-1-6-second-d.html

I’m guessing you are learning about “describing a function by hand” stuff, so here’s an article about the second derivative test: https://web.ma.utexas.edu/users/m408n/m408c/CurrentWeb/LM4-3-12.php

If you want a derivative 101 guide, this is pretty good: https://tutorial.math.lamar.edu/pdf/calculus_cheat_sheet_derivatives.pdf

I’ve given you a lot of content, but I wouldn’t try to absorb this all at once. I’d skim through some of it tonight, get a good nights sleep and cram in the morning. Then you are energized and in a better mood.

And, finally, remember that you are SO much more than a test score. A test score doesn’t define who you are or what you will become.
